content.text:
## Bottom line

**Negotiate. Don’t accept the first offer, and don’t walk away yet.**

The offer is **good in absolute terms but approximately market-median for Google L6**, rather than a premium package designed to pull a happy, compensation-sensitive Meta IC6 away. Current Levels.fyi data puts Bay Area Google L6 PM compensation around **$551,000**, almost exactly matching your offer’s $552,000 first-year target compensation. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area))

Because you weren’t looking, are happy at Meta, and would be taking refresh and organizational risk, I would want **materially more guaranteed compensation** before moving.

---

## 1. What the offer is actually worth

Assuming the $1.08 million grant vests evenly:

| Scenario | Base + bonus | Equity vesting | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Google, no refreshes | $282K | $270K | **$552K/year** |
| Meta, normalized current TC | $276K | $250K | **$526K/year** |
| Meta, next 12 months | $276K | $200K | **$476K** |

So Google is:

- **$76K, or 16%, better than your next 12 months at Meta**
- But only **$26K, or 5%, better than your stated normal Meta run rate**
- Offering a **$5K base cut**
- Providing **no sign-on**
- Relying on uncertain refreshes to make the longer-term story attractive

That is enough to make Google financially reasonable. It is **not enough to make the move obviously compelling**.

The $235K base is also only about 59% of the way through the posted $183K–$271K range. Comparable current Google Senior PM postings show similar ranges and a 20% target bonus. ([google.com](https://www.google.com/about/careers/applications/jobs/results/112598809917170374-senior-product-manager-generative-ai-google-cloud?company=Google&company=Google+Fiber&company=YouTube%C2%B0ree%3DBACHELORS&distance=50&employment_type=FULL_TIME&gclsrc=aw.ds&hl=en_US&jlo=en_US&location=United+States&page=1&q=&sort_by=date&src=Online%2FHouse+Ads%2FBKWS))

---

## 2. Treat the refresh story carefully

Under the recruiter’s illustration, your compensation would approximately be:

| Year | New-hire equity | Refresh equity vesting | Total TC |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | $270K | $0 | **$552K** |
| 2 | $270K | $62.5K | **$614.5K** |
| 3 | $270K | $125K | **$677K** |
| 4 | $270K | $187.5K | **$739.5K** |

That averages about **$646K over four years**.

But there are two important catches:

1. **The refresh grants are not guaranteed.**
2. The apparent ramp is temporary. Once the new-hire grant expires, four overlapping $250K refresh grants produce only about **$250K of annual equity vesting**, not $458K. Holding salary constant, that brings steady-state TC back to roughly **$532K**.

So the refresh illustration is not a permanent $646K–$740K compensation level. It is a temporary stacking period followed by a new-hire-grant cliff.

For decision-making, I would use:

- **Floor case:** zero refresh value
- **Conservative expected case:** credit perhaps 50% of the illustration
- **Upside case:** the full recruiter illustration

At a 50% haircut to the refresh illustration, first-four-year expected TC is only about **$599K/year**.

---

## 3. What I would ask for

Make one clear, package-level counter:

- **Base: $260,000**
- **New-hire equity: $1,400,000**
- **Sign-on bonus: $150,000**

That package is worth about **$700K/year averaged over four years**, excluding refreshes.

That is an aggressive anchor, but it is defensible because:

- You are currently at roughly $526K.
- You were recruited rather than actively searching.
- Your base would otherwise decline.
- You have meaningful near-term Meta vesting.
- Google’s refresh story is explicitly non-guaranteed.
- The opening offer is around the public L6 median, not the top of the market.
- The posted base range supports room above $235K.

Negotiation is worth attempting: research involving thousands of tech employees found that nearly half of those who negotiated improved their offers, with successful improvements averaging about 13.9% in the studied sample. ([marketing.wharton.upenn.edu](https://marketing.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Negotiations_WP.pdf))

### Reasonable settlement range

I would view this as a successful counter:

- **Base:** $250K–$255K
- **Equity:** $1.25M–$1.35M
- **Sign-on:** $100K–$150K

For example:

> $250K base + $1.3M equity + $100K sign-on

is worth about **$650K/year over the first four years**, before any refreshes.

### My approximate minimum if compensation drives the decision

I would want at least the equivalent of:

- **$250K base**
- **$1.2M equity**
- **$100K sign-on**

That is about **$625K/year over four years**, excluding refreshes.

Equivalent mixes are fine. For example, if Google won’t provide a sign-on, it should put more into the initial equity grant. If base remains $235K, I would want roughly **$1.27M equity plus $100K sign-on** merely to get to the same $625K four-year average.

---

## 4. Priority order

Ask for all three, but prioritize them as follows:

### 1. More new-hire equity

Target an increase from **$1.08M to $1.3M–$1.4M**.

This is the biggest lever and reduces your dependence on uncertain refreshes.

### 2. A sign-on bonus

Ask for **$150K**, aiming to land at **$100K or more**.

Frame it as compensation for:

- Leaving a strong position you were not planning to leave
- Transition and performance risk
- Lost or disrupted Meta vesting/bonus timing
- The lack of any guaranteed refresh compensation

Check the repayment provision; sign-ons commonly carry a one-year clawback.

### 3. Higher base

Ask for **$260K**, aiming for at least **$250K**.

Your current base is already $240K, so asking you to switch companies for a base cut is not especially compelling. Base also increases your target bonus and compounds through future adjustments.

---

## 5. Suggested wording

> I’m genuinely excited about the role and team. At the same time, I wasn’t actively looking to leave Meta, and compensation is an important part of the decision for me.
>
> My current annual compensation is approximately $526K, and I have about $200K of Meta equity vesting during the next 12 months. At the current terms, Google’s guaranteed target compensation is approximately $552K, with a lower base, no sign-on, and future refresh grants that aren’t guaranteed. That makes the move financially fairly close to staying rather than clearly compelling.
>
> To make the transition work, I’d like to ask the compensation team to consider a package of $260K base, $1.4M in new-hire equity, and a $150K sign-on bonus. I’m flexible on the mix, but I’m looking for stronger guaranteed four-year economics rather than relying primarily on potential refresh grants.
>
> If you can get meaningfully closer to that package, I’d be very interested in moving forward.

Then stop talking. Let the recruiter take it to compensation.

If they ask, “What would make you sign immediately?”, you can say:

> If we can get the guaranteed package to roughly $650K annualized over the first four years, I believe we can get to yes, subject to reviewing the final written terms.

Only say that if you really would accept around that level.

---

## 6. Accept, negotiate, or walk?

### Accept the current offer now?

**No.** You have enough leverage and too little reason to accept the first version.

### Negotiate?

**Definitely.** Your current employment and compensation are legitimate leverage, even without another outside offer. Do not bluff or invent competing offers.

### Walk away?

If Google makes no meaningful improvement, I would probably **stay at Meta**, unless the Google role is substantially better for scope, manager, promotion prospects, or personal interest.

The current offer is not bad. But for someone who:

- is already happy,
- values compensation heavily,
- is not escaping a bad situation, and
- must assume refreshes may disappoint,

a roughly **5% normalized initial premium** is not enough compensation for switching risk.

**My recommendation:** counter at **$260K / $1.4M / $150K**, target a settlement around **$250K–$255K / $1.25M–$1.35M / $100K–$150K**, and be prepared to stay at Meta if the guaranteed four-year value remains much below approximately **$625K annually**.

content.text:
## My call: **take it—if you like the role and manager reasonably well**

The revised offer has crossed from “negotiate or stay” to **financially attractive enough to accept**. Since they have explicitly called it final, I would not keep pushing unless something in the written terms differs from what you were told.

### Economics assuming even four-year RSU vesting

|  | Year 1 | Years 2–4 | Four-year total | Four-year average |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **Google** | $240K base + $48K bonus + $270K RSUs + $200K sign-on = **$758K** | **$558K/year** | **$2.432M** | **$608K/year** |
| **Meta, stated run rate** | **$526K** | **$526K/year** | **$2.104M** | **$526K/year** |
| **Difference** | **+$232K** | **+$32K/year** | **+$328K** | **+$82K/year** |

Using your actual $200K of Meta vesting in the next 12 months, Meta’s first-year compensation is approximately **$476K**. On that basis:

- Google first year: **$758K**
- Meta first year: **$476K**
- Google advantage: **$282K**
- Google four-year advantage: approximately **$378K**

These are pre-tax figures and assume the stated share values remain constant.

Your Google package averages **$608K over four years before any refreshes**, about **16% above** your normalized Meta compensation. That is also almost exactly the currently reported Bay Area median for Google L6 PM compensation, though self-reported market data mixes new hires and existing employees with accumulated refresh grants. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area?utm_source=openai))

## The important nuance

The $200K sign-on is doing most of the work.

Without it, Google’s recurring initial compensation is:

- Base: $240K
- Bonus target: $48K
- Initial RSUs: $270K
- **Recurring total: $558K**

That is only **$32K—or 6%—above Meta’s $526K**.

Therefore:

- **The first four years are attractive.**
- The permanent recurring advantage is modest.
- Longer-term upside still depends heavily on refreshes, raises, promotion, or another grant replacing the initial RSUs.
- You should not value the recruiter’s $250K refresh illustration as guaranteed compensation.

If the refresh illustration actually materializes, Google wins decisively. If refreshes are approximately half that level, Google still looks good. If refreshes are zero, the first four years remain better because of the sign-on, but you would face a major equity cliff after the initial grant finishes.

## Conditions I would verify before signing

Get these answered from the **actual written agreements**, not just verbally:

1. **Exact RSU vesting schedule**  
   Confirm whether it is $270K-equivalent each year or front-loaded, and the first vest date.

2. **RSU valuation mechanics**  
   Confirm how the $1.08M is converted into shares and which stock-price averaging period is used.

3. **Sign-on payment timing**  
   Is the entire $200K paid shortly after starting, or split over multiple payments?

4. **Sign-on repayment terms**  
   Confirm:
   - How long the repayment period lasts
   - Whether repayment is prorated monthly
   - What happens if Google lays you off or terminates you without cause
   - Whether repayment is based on the gross or net amount
   - Whether the agreement permits deferral or another payment structure

   California rules concerning repayment provisions have changed recently, so the language of your specific agreement matters; don’t rely on generic assumptions about a standard one-year clawback. ([dir.ca.gov](https://www.dir.ca.gov/chswc/meetings/2026/04-08-26-Item-7a-Leg-Update.pdf?utm_source=openai))

5. **First-year bonus eligibility**  
   Confirm whether the 20% target is prorated based on your start date and whether you must remain employed through a particular payout date.

6. **Any Meta compensation you would still receive**  
   Determine whether you would retain a prorated Meta bonus, vest anything before departure, or lose additional compensation not included in the $200K figure.

## When I would still stay at Meta

I would reject Google despite the money if any of these are true:

- You are materially less excited about the Google product or manager.
- The role’s scope looks weaker than your current IC6 scope.
- You expect to leave Google within the sign-on repayment period.
- You have strong evidence that a Meta promotion or significant retention grant is imminent.
- Your current Meta job has substantially better work-life balance, organizational influence, or promotion trajectory.
- You value your known environment enough that a roughly $80K annualized four-year premium does not compensate for switching risk.

## Recommendation

**Accept, provided the role and manager clear your bar and the written sign-on terms are reasonable.**

You successfully converted a merely adequate offer into one that:

- Keeps your base whole
- Fully offsets the stated $200K of near-term Meta RSUs with cash
- Pays approximately **$608K annually over four years before refreshes**
- Gives you substantial refresh upside without requiring refreshes for the initial four-year package to beat staying

I would **not reopen compensation negotiations** after they labeled this their best offer. Review the documents, clarify the six items above, and then either accept cleanly or decline because you prefer Meta—not as another negotiating tactic.
